title: Benchmark Protocols & Load Generation Workshop — Rho Systems
next_steps: Redwood to share canonical benchmark repo and load profiles (k6 + JMeter)
Rho Systems to run warm/cold runs with customer prompt set and share logs
Schedule follow-up to review initial metrics and tune batching/caching (w/in 1 week)
Redwood to provide suggested quantization config and recommended NVLink topology notes
action_items: Marcus Chen - push benchmark harness to https://github.com/redwood/benchmarks/rho - 2025-12-05
Anya Feldman - export 10k sample prompts from prod and upload to secure drive - 2025-12-04
Priya Nair - provide VPC peering diagram and firewall rules checklist - 2025-12-06
transcript:
[00:00:00] Lydia Park: ok, uh, thanks everyone for joining. I see Carlos, Anya, Tom, great. We scheduled an hour to go deep on benchmarking methodology — standardized prompts, load generation, and how to make an apples to not-apples, uh, like actually apples-to-apples comparison across hosted and on-prem.
[00:00:18] Carlos Medina: yeah thanks Lydia. we want something repeatable — our infra team gets nervous when benchmarks aren't comparable. we run different GPUs in prod and staging, so we want to nail down the protocol.
[00:00:28] Marcus Chen: cool, i'll kick off with a quick agenda: objectives, traceable prompt sets, load generator choices (k6/locust/jmeter), warm vs steady-state, metrics to collect (p50/p95/p99 latencies, tokens/sec, GPU util, power), and then specific config for KV cache and batching.
[00:00:45] Anya Feldman: quick note — our main constraint is 95th percentile latency under 250ms for short completions and under 800ms for longer multi-token responses. throughput is secondary but still important.
[00:00:55] Tom Baker: also security — VPC peering, customer-managed KMS for keys; on-prem option may change perf due to RDMA/PCIe layout differences.
[00:01:05] Marcus Chen: totally. one of our big goals today is to define the "same experiment" semantics. same model file version, same tokenizer, same max_seq, same sampling params, same prompt pre- and post-processing. even things like EOS handling or trailing whitespace can change token counts.
[00:01:22] Lydia Park: right — we want to avoid hidden variable bias. so action 1 is a canonical prompt schema.
[00:01:27] [00:01:30] Speaker 1: (background) yeah
[00:01:31] Marcus Chen: starting with prompt sets — we recommend two tiers: 1) production sample set (Anya, you export a representative sample, stratified by length and use-case), and 2) synthetic distribution that matches token length histogram (we'll provide a generator). reason: synthetic lets you sweep loads deterministically.
[00:01:48] Anya Feldman: for production samples, do you want de-identified inputs or raw? we have PII redaction to consider.
[00:01:54] Lydia Park: de-id is fine. include metadata: intended model endpoint, avg response tokens, and success criteria label (pass/fail) so we can tie quality regressions back to prompts.
[00:02:05] Marcus Chen: on load generation: we suggest k6 for cloud-hosted, JMeter for teams that need heavy TLS features, and Locust for complex user-journey simulations. importantly, the clients must be run from a separate machine (not on the same host as the model) to avoid CPU/network interference.
[00:02:20] Tom Baker: what about the request pattern? constant RPS vs Poisson vs closed loop?
[00:02:24] Marcus Chen: good question. we recommend two modes: burst/ramp for stress tests (ramp 0 -> target in 5 minutes, hold 10 minutes, ramp down) and steady-state (ramp to target, then hold 30 minutes) to capture KV cache warmup and persistent batching behavior. Poisson is useful for emulating user traffic.
[00:02:40] [00:02:42] Anya Feldman: how do we measure warm vs cold cache? our prod has lots of prefix overlap so warm cache looks much faster.
[00:02:47] Marcus Chen: we define cold as the very first pass after model spin-up with empty KV; warm as after N unique prefixes have been run (we usually pick 10k unique prompts or until p95 stabilizes). for prefix caching, measure both prefix-hit and hit-rate over time. instrument the server to emit cache_hits/cache_misses per request.
[00:03:05] Lydia Park: also track KV cache eviction events and shard locality — on-prem NVLink topologies could keep KV local and give better latency than a multi-node cloud setup.
[00:03:14] Tom Baker: what telemetry do you recommend for on-prem? we have Prometheus + Grafana.
[00:03:18] Marcus Chen: Prometheus is perfect. export: per-request latency histograms, tokens generated, batch sizes, GPU utilization, tensor memory (KV size), PCIe stalls, and NVLink link counters if available. add power draw if you can. we provide a Grafana dashboard template.
[00:03:34] [00:03:36] Carlos Medina: sampling randomness affects latency — greedy vs temperature-based sampling can change tokens per second. how do we keep comparability?
[00:03:43] Marcus Chen: lock sampling parameters across runs. for apples-to-apples, run deterministic sampling (greedy or fixed seed) for latency comparisons. then run separate quality runs with temperature/sampling to see throughput under production sampling. report both.
[00:03:57] Anya Feldman: ok. what about quantization? our models have been converted to int8 for cost. that changes both perf and quality.
[00:04:04] Priya Nair: quantization is a big confounder. document: quantization algorithm (PTQ vs QAT), format (INT8, Q4_0, Q4_1, FP16), and any per-layer remapping. we should run baseline FP16, then Q* variants, and report delta in latency and any perplexity or eval metric change on a holdout set.
[00:04:20] Marcus Chen: we recommend at least FP16 and the customer's preferred quant format. if using LLM.int8 or per-channel sym/asym quant, note the kernel implementation—different runtimes implement int8 matmul differently and can give wildly different perf.
[00:04:33] [00:04:35] Tom Baker: on-prem GPUs are A100 80GB NVLink, cloud is A10G. should we expect 2x difference?
[00:04:41] Marcus Chen: depends. NVLink improves KV exchange for multi-GPU generation. for single-GPU, A100 may be faster but kernel availability matters. measure tokens/sec per GPU and normalized latency per token. we recommend reporting cost-normalized metrics later (e.g., latency per $0.01 of GPU time).
[00:04:57] Lydia Park: let's put that in the protocol: always report raw latency distribution plus normalized metrics: latency per token and tokens/sec per dollar.
[00:05:05] [00:05:06] Anya Feldman: how do we handle different context windows? our fine-tuned model uses 8k context; some open models are 16k.
[00:05:11] Marcus Chen: set a fixed max_context for the benchmark. if you must compare across windows, run separate experiments at 2k, 8k, 16k and make it explicit. also make sure tokenization is consistent: same tokenizer version and pre-tokenization script.
[00:05:25] Carlos Medina: can you describe the canonical measurement phases?
[00:05:28] Marcus Chen: sure — Phase 0: Environment sanity (verify kernel versions, CUDA, NCCL, OS). Phase 1: Cold start single-request latency (spin up model and send a single request). Phase 2: KV warmup (run stratified prompts until metrics stabilize). Phase 3: Steady-state throughput (hold target RPS for 30 min). Phase 4: Stress test (ramp to max and observe degradation/failover). Phase 5: Recovery and canary fallbacks.
[00:05:50] [00:05:52] Priya Nair: include background noise tests — run co-located CPU jobs to simulate noisy neighbors if you plan to multi-tenant.
[00:05:58] Marcus Chen: yes. and for dedicated capacity, measure tail latency under sustained high batch sizes; batching improves throughput but can spike p95. we should tune max batching window and batching latency budget.
[00:06:10] Anya Feldman: can you explain continuous batching? i saw that in the docs but not sure how it plays with KV caching.
[00:06:15] Marcus Chen: continuous batching accumulates in-flight requests and executes them together to maximize GPU utilization. KV cache requires per-request KV addressing but when requests share prefixes, we can stitch outputs and reuse cached KV. the risk: if you batch long and you need low single-request latency, p95 increases. protocol: report the batching config used (max_batch_size, max_latency_ms, batching_strategy) and the observed effective batch distribution.
[00:06:34] [00:06:36] Tom Baker: are there recommended synthetic distributions for prompt lengths? 
[00:06:39] Marcus Chen: yes — use a mixture distribution that mirrors your prod hist: 50% short (<32 tokens), 30% medium (32-256), 20% long (>256). sample from log-normal for token length within each bucket to avoid uniform extremes.
[00:06:53] Anya Feldman: prompt seeds — do we randomize or use fixed seeds?
[00:06:56] Marcus Chen: use a fixed seed for deterministic benchmarking; for robustness runs, randomize across N seeds and report mean+std.
[00:07:03] [00:07:05] Carlos Medina: what about tooling for comparing traces? we currently use JFrog logs and Splunk.
[00:07:09] Marcus Chen: export request-level traces as JSON lines with fields: timestamp, prompt_id, prompt_length, response_tokens, latency_ms, batch_id, cache_hit, host_id, gpu_id, kernel_version. then ingest into Splunk/ELK and correlate with GPU metrics. we'll share a mapping schema.
[00:07:24] Lydia Park: i'll note the artifacts link: https://drive.redwood/inference/benchmark-protocols/rho-workshop (we'll share access) and the repo: https://github.com/redwood/benchmarks/rho.
[00:07:35] [00:07:37] Anya Feldman: security again — if we run private on VPC, do you need mirror images? how does telemetry get out?
[00:07:41] Priya Nair: for VPC deploys, we ship a private collector that pushes metrics over an encrypted channel to the customer's Prometheus or to a pushgateway behind their firewall. logs and models stay in customer-controlled storage; keys are customer-managed KMS/HSM. we also support an air-gapped install for compliance — but that increases overhead for us to triage kernels.
[00:07:59] Tom Baker: air-gapped operations probably will change benchmarking cadence — we'll need to plan sync windows. noted.
[00:08:05] Marcus Chen: another important point: make sure all runs use the same CPU/GPU driver stack and the same BLAS/Kernel libs. different cuBLAS, CUBLASLt, or oneDNN versions can change perf. we capture driver versions in the experiment metadata.
[00:08:20] [00:08:22] Carlos Medina: latency SLOs — how do you account for tail jitter from noisy neighbor?
[00:08:26] Marcus Chen: report both raw tails and a noise-controlled tail: run an isolated test with no other workloads and a co-located test. the delta tells you jitter from noisy neighbors. also include per-core CPU utilization; sometimes CPU saturation on the server causes RPC queuing.
[00:08:39] Anya Feldman: do you recommend a standard set of metrics output?
[00:08:42] Marcus Chen: yes — we use: request_id, timestamp_iso, prompt_tokens, response_tokens, latency_ms, status (200/500), cache_hit (true/false), batch_size, model_version, quant_format, gpu_util_pct, mem_used_mb, host_id, zone. export as ndjson.
[00:08:56] [00:08:57] Lydia Park: let's talk about evaluation for quality regressions — perplexity is ok, but we also need prompt-level reference metrics.
[00:09:02] Marcus Chen: agree. have a small labeled eval set (500-2k prompts) with human judgments or programmatic checks (BLEU/ROUGE/semantic similarity). compare outputs from each quantization/model variant. flag drop in pass-rate > 1.5% as an alert.
[00:09:16] Carlos Medina: how do we reproduce results from the cloud hosted Redwood API vs on-prem? we expect different latencies but want the delta to be attributable.
[00:09:22] Marcus Chen: run the exact same harness, record infrastructure metadata (GPU type, kernel versions, NVLink topology), and use a canonical mapping table we provide to normalize. optionally, you can run a cost-normalized baseline by computing latency at $/token. but remember: data plane locality (VPC vs internet hop) will affect network latencies. measure RTT separately.
[00:09:40] [00:09:42] Tom Baker: any gotchas about serverless-hosted models or autoscaling?
[00:09:45] Marcus Chen: autoscaling can hide cold starts; include a cold-start phase and also simulate pod churn. for serverless we instrument container startup time, model load time, and first-request latency.
[00:09:55] Anya Feldman: how about kv cache consistency across nodes? if we have sharded KV, prefix matching might fail.
[00:10:00] Marcus Chen: yes — sharded KV requires consistent hash routing by session or by prefix. for bench we recommend using session pinning to a GPU to simplify measurements, then run a multi-shard test that exercises cross-shard routing and observe added latency.
[00:10:13] [00:10:15] Carlos Medina: do you support synthetic token generation to stress KV? we can craft prompts to produce many unique tokens and force evictions.
[00:10:20] Marcus Chen: yes, we have a synthetic generator that can produce long unique prefixes to drive KV growth. we'll add that to the repo.
[00:10:25] [00:10:27] Priya Nair: let's cover replication and fallback: if a node fails, do you have an automatic fallback to a smaller model?
[00:10:31] Marcus Chen: Redwood supports policy-based fallbacks — A/B canary or fallback to a cheaper quantized variant. include failure scenarios in stress tests and measure failover latency and error rates.
[00:10:41] Lydia Park: ok, time check — ~44 minutes left? actually we've been running 10 minutes, wait, math is off, we started at 14:00 so running 10 minutes — our duration is 54 so we have lots left.
[00:10:52] [00:10:54] Anya Feldman: can we get an example runbook for the benchmark? step-by-step with commands?
[00:10:59] Marcus Chen: yes. minimal runbook: 1) record environment (nvidia-smi, nvlink topo), 2) checkout repo, 3) prepare prompt dataset, 4) run cold start test: python run_single_request.py --model X, 5) run warmup: ./bench warmup --dataset prompts.csv --unique 10k, 6) run steady-state: k6 run --vus X --duration 30m --rps Y, 7) collect traces: ./collect_traces.sh > traces.ndjson, 8) run quality eval: python eval_quality.py --ref eval_set.json. we'll drop this in the repo.
[00:11:29] [00:11:31] Tom Baker: looking at timelines, can we get initial runs done next week? we have a maintenance window Friday.
[00:11:36] Lydia Park: yes that's feasible. Marcus and Priya will share artifacts by Friday EOD. Anya will run the extraction and start with a 5k sample.
[00:11:45] [00:11:47] Carlos Medina: any notes about benchmarking multi-tenant vs dedicated? we might do dedicated for a pilot.
[00:11:51] Marcus Chen: dedicated simplifies tail management; multi-tenant needs stricter isolation and noisier tails. for dedicated compare: baseline latency with no other services, then add controlled background workloads (cpu stress, mem hog) to quantify tail increase.
[00:12:03] Anya Feldman: one more thing: tokenization differences across frameworks — HF tokenizer vs custom tokenizer — we must lock that.
[00:12:09] Marcus Chen: lock tokenizer class and version. if you have custom pre-tokenization steps, keep a canonical script checked into the repo and apply it to all prompts before measuring.
[00:12:17] [00:12:19] Priya Nair: i will also include a checklist for firewall ports (gRPC/TCP) and recommended MTU for RDMA.
[00:12:25] Marcus Chen: good. and we'll provide an example NVLink topology note: on a 4x A100 box, ensure GPU affinity across worker threads to avoid cross-socket PCIe penalties.
[00:12:36] [00:12:38] Carlos Medina: let's capture acceptance criteria: p95 <= 250ms for short completions and end-to-end success rate > 99% under steady-state target of 200 rps.
[00:12:48] Lydia Park: noted — we'll include acceptance criteria in the protocol doc.
[00:12:52] [00:12:54] Anya Feldman: small question: how do you ensure reproducible floating point behavior across hosts? different drivers can cause tiny numerical diffs.
[00:13:00] Marcus Chen: capture libc/cuda driver versions; for quality comparisons use deterministic seeds and ideally run multiple repetitions to get confidence intervals. don't over-interpret tiny numeric differences; focus on functional metrics and human judgement.
[00:13:12] [00:13:14] Tom Baker: any special housekeeping for logs to avoid PII leaking in traces?
[00:13:18] Marcus Chen: scrub prompts at ingest stage; use prompt_id and hashed prompt reference in the trace rather than full text. for benchmark quality runs we can use de-id datasets.
[00:13:27] [00:13:29] Lydia Park: ok wrapping up — recap and owners. Marcus to publish the harness and runbook, Priya to add VPC/firewall checklist, Anya to export sample prompts. we'll reconvene next Wednesday to review initial run outputs.
[00:13:44] Carlos Medina: great, that sounds good. thanks everyone.
[00:13:47] [00:13:49] Speaker 2: thanks
[00:13:50] Lydia Park: thanks, talk soon.
[00:13:52] END: approximate transcript end — note transcription may have small errors (mis-attributed speakers, minor word swaps)
